full_judgment:
ATM Afzal CJ: These six appeals by the pre-emptor appellants, following leave, arise out of a judgment and order dated 21 July, 1985 passed by a Single Judge of the High Court Division (at Comilla) making the Rules absolute in Civil Revision Nos. 40-45 of 1985 and restoring the judgment and order of the trial Court after setting aside those of the lower appellate Court passed in six pre-emption cases filed by the appellants under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 against six different sets of opposite-party-respondents. 

 7. It appears that the learned Judge of the High Court Division refused to interfere with the finding of the lower appellate Court that the applications for pre-emption were not barred by limitation but the learned Judge reversed the decision of the lower appellate Court on the ground that it was wrongly held by the said Court that the pre-emptors had locus standi to file the applications for pre-emption. The learned Judge observed that the lower appellate Court had committed an error of law apparent on the face of the record by failing to appreciate the burden of proof in the present case. The preempted-respondents positively stated in their written objection that the pre-emptors had sold out all their shares in the case holding and they had no locus standi to prefer the application for pre-emption. The learned Judge observed that pre-emptor No. 1 deposing as PW 1 completely yielded to the assertion of the preempted-respondents in his cross-examination and therefore, they (the pre-empties) had no further burden to prove that the pre-emptors had sold out all their shares in the case holding. The burden of proof lay with the pre-emptors to prove that they still retained some shares in the case Khatian in order to be able to ask for pre-emption as co-sharers. The learned Judge further observed that the lower appellate Court had misread the evidence of PW 1 in that the witness never stated that he was an existing co-sharer in the case Khatian, but he merely stated that it was not a fact that he was not a co-sharer. This was an expression of opinion as to his status in the case holding and not a statement of fact, the learned Judge held. It was finally held that the trial Court had correctly found that the pre-emptors had disqualified themselves by making a blatant admission that they had sold out all their (share of) lands in the case Khatian. 

 9. Mr. Abdul Baset Majumder, learned Advocate for the appellants, submits that there is no assertion by the pre-emptees in their written objection that the pre-emptors had sold out all their shares in the case holding nor PW 1 had made any such statement in his cross-examination as wrongly found by the High Court Division. Mr. Sharifuddin Chaklader, learned Advocate-on-Record for the respondents, submits that he also does not find any such statement in the written objection of the pre-emptees. Upon going through the written objection we have rather found that the pre-emptees themselves alleged that the pre-emptors had sold out most of their lands in the disputed Mouza and thereby got huge money and having become greedy for the disputed lands filed the present cases falsely in collusion with and with the monetary help of opposite Parties No. 4-6. 

 10. PW 1 Chandra Nath Sutradhar in his cross-examination stated thus: 

 12. It is apparent from the above that the learned Assistant Judge totally misread the evidence of PW 1 in that he never stated that he had sold his entire share in the case holding for making deposit in the case nor had he said that he had no share in the disputed holding. The finding of the learned Assistant Judge that the pre-emptors had divested themselves of all their interest in the disputed holding and thus lost their locus standi to claim pre-emption is founded upon total misreading of the evidence of PW 1. It has been noticed that PW 1 stoutly denied the suggestion that he had sold all his interest in the disputed jama or that he had ceased to be a co-sharer therein. In view of the aforesaid facts which are on record Mr. Sharifuddin Chaklader has found it difficult to support the impugned judgment which has been patently passed upon a misreading of the written objection of the pro-emptees by the learned Judge himself and further upon misreading of evidence of PW 1 by the trial Court which was wrongly relied upon by the learned Judge.
